title: Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding
claim: Models fail despite decisive evidence due to linguistic and visual shortcut biases; steering the representation away from them restores correct predictions.
layout: 3 zones, left-to-right: video frame examples, failure box, vector diagram plus bar charts
description: The left side shows two rows of video frames separated by a dashed line, with bounding boxes marking evidence. Green boxes mark correct evidence and red boxes mark misleading salient regions. The first row is a wedding scene and the second is a Tom and Jerry cartoon. Beside each row is a multiple-choice question with the correct answer in green and the wrong answer in red. A central box lists GPT-4o, Qwen3-VL and InternVL-3 with the red text 'MLLMs FAILED!'. After a vertical dotted divider, a vector diagram shows the 'Full View' vector pushed by 'Linguistic bias' (α1) and 'Visual bias' (α2) toward 'Full View after Intervention'. Two bar charts at the far right show the wrong answer (red) dominating before the intervention and the correct answer (green) dominating after it. The eye goes first to the colorful frames and the red 'FAILED!' text.
caption: MLLMs often fail despite the presence of decisive evidence, either by following spurious linguistic correlations or by over-relying on salient but misleading visual observations. CLEAR diagnoses these shortcut-biased trajectories with controlled probes and steers the full-video representation toward evidence-consistent prediction.
abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, i.e., the misleading cues caused by spurious linguistic correlations and salient yet irrelevant visual observations. In this paper, we first introduce S-MME, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
